def: A truth table lists all possible truth values (T or F) of statements, and shows the result of combining them with connectives like and, or, not, implies, iff.
points: A simple statement is either True (T) or False (F), never both.
and (^) is true only when both parts are true.
or (v) is true when at least one part is true.
not (~) flips the truth value: ~T = F, ~T = F.
implies (->) is false only when the first part is T and second is F; otherwise true.
iff (<->) is true when both parts have the same truth value.
For n statements, a truth table has 2^n rows.
formula: p -> q is false only when p = T and q = F

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["List all T F combos"] --> B["Apply connective"]
  B --> C["Fill result column"]
  C --> D["Read truth values row by row"]

example: For p = T, q = F: p^q = F, p v q = T, ~p = F, p -> q = F, p <-> q = F.
tip: Always write the full table with all rows; examiners give marks for each correct row, not just the final answer.

def: A statement pattern is a tautology if always true, a contradiction if always false, and a contingency if it is sometimes true and sometimes false.
points: Build the complete truth table for the statement pattern.
Look at the final result column only.
If every entry is T, it is a tautology.
If every entry is F, it is a contradiction.
If the column has a mix of T and F, it is a contingency.
Tautologies are useful to prove logical laws are always valid.
formula: All T = tautology; all F = contradiction; mixed = contingency

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Final column of truth table"] --> B["All T"]
  A --> C["All F"]
  A --> D["Mixed T and F"]
  B --> E["Tautology"]
  C --> F["Contradiction"]
  D --> G["Contingency"]

example: p v ~p: for p=T, ~p=F, p v ~p=T. For p=F, ~p=T, p v ~p=T. All T, so it is a tautology.
tip: State the name clearly (tautology/contradiction/contingency) in your final line — this is a separate mark.

t: Logical equivalence and De Morgan's laws
def: Two statements are logically equivalent if their truth tables give identical results in every row. De Morgan's laws relate negation of and/or statements.
points: Make truth tables of both statements side by side.
Compare the final columns row by row.
If every row matches, the statements are equivalent, written p === q.
De Morgan's law 1: ~(p ^ q) = ~p v ~q.
De Morgan's law 2: ~(p v q) = ~p ^ ~q.
These laws let you simplify complicated negated statements.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Statement 1 table"] --> C["Compare columns"]
  B["Statement 2 table"] --> C
  C --> D["Match every row"]
  D --> E["Logically equivalent"]

example: Check ~(p^q) and ~p v ~q for p=T,q=F: p^q=F so ~(p^q)=T. ~p=F, ~q=T so ~p v ~q=T. Both T, matches De Morgan's law.
tip: Write out both tables fully side by side before concluding equivalence — partial checking loses marks.

def: For a conditional statement p -> q, the converse swaps the parts, the inverse negates both parts, and the contrapositive negates and swaps both parts.
points: Original statement: p -> q.
Converse: q -> p (swap only).
Inverse: ~p -> ~q (negate only).
Contrapositive: ~q -> ~p (negate and swap).
The contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original statement.
The converse and inverse are logically equivalent to each other but not to the original.
formula: p -> q  ;  converse q -> p  ;  inverse ~p -> ~q  ;  contrapositive ~q -> ~p

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["p implies q"] --> B["Converse: q implies p"]
  A --> C["Inverse: not p implies not q"]
  A --> D["Contrapositive: not q implies not p"]

example: p: it rains, q: ground is wet. Converse: if ground is wet, it rains. Inverse: if it does not rain, ground is not wet. Contrapositive: if ground is not wet, it did not rain.
tip: Clearly label each of the three statements separately — this is a standard 2-mark question.

def: Quantifiers state whether a condition holds for all elements (universal) or for at least one element (existential). Duality swaps ^ with v and T with F in a statement pattern.
points: Universal quantifier: for all x, written (for all x).
Existential quantifier: there exists x, written (there exists x).
Negation of 'for all x, p(x)' is 'there exists x, ~p(x)'.
Negation of 'there exists x, p(x)' is 'for all x, ~p(x)'.
Dual of a statement is formed by replacing ^ with v, v with ^, T with F, and F with T.
Duality is used to quickly derive a related true statement.
formula: ~(for all x, p(x)) = there exists x, ~p(x)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["For all x p of x"] -->|negate| B["There exists x not p of x"]
  C["There exists x p of x"] -->|negate| D["For all x not p of x"]

example: Negate 'for all x in N, x > 0': result is 'there exists x in N such that x is not greater than 0' i.e. x <= 0.
tip: Remember quantifier negation flips the quantifier type AND negates the inner statement, both steps are needed for marks.

def: A switching circuit can be represented by a logical statement: switches in series behave like AND (^), switches in parallel behave like OR (v).
points: Each switch is either closed (T, current flows) or open (F, no current).
Series connection: current flows only if both switches are closed, so it is p ^ q.
Parallel connection: current flows if either switch is closed, so it is p v q.
Write the circuit as a logical expression using ^ and v.
Simplify the expression using logical laws to design an equivalent simpler circuit.
The simplified expression tells you the minimum switches needed.
formula: Series = p ^ q (AND)     Parallel = p v q (OR)

diagram.draw: Draw a battery on the left connected by wires. For series: draw two switches p and q one after another on a single wire path to the bulb. For parallel: draw two separate wire branches, each with one switch (p and q), both branches meeting at the bulb.

example: Circuit with switches p, (p ^ q) v (p ^ ~q) simplifies using distributive law to p ^ (q v ~q) = p ^ T = p, meaning only switch p is needed.
tip: Draw the circuit diagram neatly with labelled switches — the diagram itself usually carries a separate mark.
